title: Sigmoid and caecal volvulus
subtitle: Decompress the sigmoid, resect the caecum

sources.org: American Society of Colon and Rectal Surgeons (ASCRS)
sources.title: Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Colonic Volvulus and Acute Colonic Pseudo-Obstruction
WSES consensus guidelines on sigmoid volvulus management

red_flags.text: Peritonitis, fever, tachycardia, raised lactate or free air: suspect gangrene or perforation. This patient goes to theatre, not to endoscopy.
Dark, haemorrhagic or ulcerated mucosa at endoscopic decompression: ischaemia, abandon decompression and operate.
Massive caecal distension with right iliac fossa tenderness: impending caecal perforation.
A frail elderly patient whose symptoms are atypical: volvulus in nursing-home residents and patients with neurological disease often presents late and quietly.

do_now.text: Resuscitate with intravenous fluids, correct electrolytes, nasogastric decompression if vomiting, and urinary catheter.
CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast to confirm the diagnosis, distinguish sigmoid from caecal volvulus, and look for ischaemia or perforation.
Sigmoid volvulus without peritonitis or ischaemia: urgent endoscopic detorsion and decompression, usually by flexible sigmoidoscopy, with mucosal assessment.
Peritonitis, perforation or ischaemia: emergency laparotomy and resection without attempting endoscopic decompression.

assess.text: Peritoneal signs, physiology and lactate decide the route: endoscopy or theatre.
Frailty and goals of care, recorded early. Many patients with sigmoid volvulus are elderly with neurological or psychiatric comorbidity.
Risk of emergency laparotomy if surgery is likely.

investigate.text: FBC, U&E, CRP, lactate, group and save.
CT with intravenous contrast: whirl sign, bird's beak, absent wall enhancement, pneumatosis and portal venous gas.
Plain radiograph may show the coffee-bean sign of sigmoid volvulus, but CT is the test that changes management.
Endoscopic mucosal assessment at the time of sigmoid decompression.

resuscitate.text: After successful sigmoid decompression, leave a rectal decompression tube in place temporarily to reduce early recurrence.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics per local protocol for suspected ischaemia or perforation, before theatre.

definitive.text: Sigmoid volvulus after successful decompression: sigmoid colectomy during the same admission in fit patients, because recurrence after decompression alone is high.
Gangrenous or perforated sigmoid: resection, usually Hartmann's procedure in the unstable or contaminated patient; primary anastomosis only in a stable patient with a healthy field.
Caecal volvulus: endoscopic detorsion is not recommended; right hemicolectomy is the operation, with primary anastomosis in a stable patient or an ileostomy when unstable or contaminated.
Caecopexy or detorsion alone is not recommended for caecal volvulus because of recurrence.
Patients unfit for resection after sigmoid decompression: discuss alternatives such as percutaneous endoscopic colostomy in specialist settings, accepting the limited evidence.

escalate.text: Consultant surgeon for any volvulus with signs of ischaemia, and before deciding not to resect after decompression.
Endoscopist out of hours for sigmoid decompression; if none is available, a consultant decision on rigid sigmoidoscopy or surgery.
Critical care for perforation, sepsis or a high predicted mortality.
Palliative care input for frail patients in whom resection is not appropriate.

notes: Sigmoid and caecal volvulus are different diseases. The sigmoid is decompressed first and resected later; the caecum goes straight to resection.
Decompression without a plan for resection is a plan for readmission. The recurrence after decompression alone is the reason to operate on the same admission.
Look at the mucosa, not just at the gas. Successful detorsion of ischaemic bowel does not make it viable.
